sections.executive_summary:
Texas does not issue a separate "home care" or "companion care" license. A business that sends caregivers into homes to help with bathing, dressing, grooming, toileting, transfers or other personal care must hold a **Home and Community Support Services Agency (HCSSA) license** with the **personal assistance services (PAS)** category, issued by HHSC under Health & Safety Code Chapter 142 and 26 TAC Chapter 558 [S1][S3][S12]. Sitter-companion, chore or household services that involve no personal care are exempt from licensure [S13], but most agencies need the PAS category because clients and payers expect hands-on help.

The license costs **$2,625** and is renewed every three years for the same fee [S2]. HHSC has up to 45 days to find a complete application complete and up to 45 more days to issue the license [S4]. After licensure the agency must admit at least one client and request its initial survey on Form 2020 within six months [S5]. The administrator of a PAS-only agency needs only a high school diploma or GED plus one year of experience caring for people with functional disabilities (or two years of college in a health field) [S6], and no RN supervisor is required for PAS-only licensure [S9].

Money comes from two very different streams:

- **Private pay.** Texas families paid a median of **$30 per hour** for non-medical in-home care in 2025, one of the lowest prices in the country (rank 43) [S26].
- **Medicaid attendant care.** STAR+PLUS managed care plans pay **$4.40 per 15 minutes ($17.60/hour)** for agency-option PAS and $4.46 for Community First Choice PAS, effective September 1, 2025 [S20]. HHSC built that rate on an average attendant wage of **$13.00** plus 14% payroll taxes and benefits, leaving $0.69 per 15 minutes ($2.76/hour) for everything else [S20][S21]. HHSC also contracts directly for Primary Home Care, Community Attendant Services and Family Care at **$17.13 per hour** (non-priority) or $17.31 (priority) [S23][S67]. All Medicaid attendant visits must be recorded in EVV, and claims without a matching EVV visit are denied or recouped [S24][S41].

The math is blunt. At the modeled wages and overhead, a **40-client private-pay agency** nets about **$14,500 a month (16.8%)** at 90% census and breaks even near 54% (Section 8). A STAR+PLUS-only agency earns only about $86 per client per month after attendant pay and per-client costs (about $48 under the lower PHC/CAS/FC rate), so it loses money at 100 clients and would need roughly 500 clients to cover a lean office — or attendant pay below the $13.00 the rate assumes. The recommended path is to launch private pay first and add STAR+PLUS volume only once the office is paid for.
sections.service_model:
### Who is served
PAS agencies help older adults and people with disabilities who live at home with activities of daily living. Texas defines **personal care** as bathing, dressing, grooming, feeding, exercising, toileting, positioning, help with self-administered medications, routine hair and skin care, and transfer or ambulation [S12]. **Personal assistance services** cover that personal care plus certain health-related tasks that are not professional nursing or that an RN delegates or determines need no delegation, including respite [S12][S9]. Texas has 31.7 million residents; 14.9% are 65 or older and 8.7% are under 65 with a disability [S49].

### License category
HCSSA licenses come in six categories; **personal assistance services** is one of them [S3]. HHSC does not require an agency to hold more than one category if its category covers the services it provides [S3]. An agency that will also provide skilled nursing or therapy needs a home health category instead (see the Texas Home Health bundle).

What does **not** need a license: sitter-companion, chore or household services that involve no personal care, health or health-related services; individuals hired and paid directly by the client or family; employees of a consumer under consumer-directed services; and registries that only connect families with caregivers and don't employ, pay or keep client records [S13].

### Service model rules (26 TAC §558.404)
- Every client gets an **individualized service plan** based on an on-site visit by the supervisor, signed by the client or family and the agency, listing services, frequency, duration, start date, charges and a plan of supervision [S9].
- A **supervisor** must be a licensed nurse or have completed two years of full-time college; a high school graduate may substitute one year of full-time supervisory employment for each required college year [S9].
- **Attendants** must be at least 18 (or a high school graduate/vocational student) and demonstrate competency when education and experience don't establish it. G-tube feedings and medication administration need an RN-, physician- or PA-led training program with a 100% written test and skills check [S9].

### Medicaid programs an agency can serve
- **STAR+PLUS** (managed care for adults 21+ who are older or have disabilities): PAS for state plan (non-HCBS) members, PAS and respite for HCBS members, and Community First Choice PAS/habilitation. MCO service coordinators authorize and monitor services [S63][S20].
- **Primary Home Care (PHC), Community Attendant Services (CAS) and Family Care (FC)**: HHSC fee-for-service programs under one HHSC contract, delivered by HCSSAs licensed for licensed home health, licensed and certified home health, or PAS [S23][S51]. PHC/CAS clients need at least 6 hours of service a week (with exceptions) and are capped at 42 hours a week (priority) or 50 hours (non-priority) [S18].

**Pending change:** HHSC published proposed amendments to Chapter 558 in the September 18, 2026 Texas Register; check the adopted text before you file [S14].
sections.licensing_pathway:
### Step 1 — Decide whether you need a license
If any caregiver will touch the client for bathing, dressing, toileting, transfers or other personal care, you need the PAS category. Companion/sitter/chore-only businesses are exempt but cannot advertise or deliver personal care [S12][S13].

### Step 2 — Form the business and get in good standing
Form a Texas LLC or corporation (Form 205 for an LLC, $300) [S46], obtain an EIN [S47], and register with the Comptroller. HHSC requires the applicant to be registered with and in good standing with both the Comptroller and the Secretary of State [S1].

### Step 3 — Qualify the administrator and alternate
- **Qualifications (PAS-only):** high school diploma or GED plus one year of experience or training caring for people with functional disabilities; or two years of full-time college in a health-related field; or the home health administrator qualifications [S6]. Both must read, write and understand English [S6].
- **Presurvey Training:** the administrator and alternate must complete HHSC's computer-based Presurvey Training **before** applying [S3][S1].
- **Administrator training:** first-time administrators need 8 clock hours before designation and 16 more within 12 months (24 total); Presurvey Training does not count [S7]. After that, 12 hours of continuing education a year [S8].

### Step 4 — Apply in TULIP
Submit the application, documents and the **$2,625** fee in TULIP [S1][S2]. HHSC has up to 45 days to determine the application is complete; if HHSC sends a notice of missing information, you have 30 days to submit it or HHSC may deny the application (and keep the fee) [S68]; after a complete response HHSC has up to 45 days to issue or deny [S4][S1]. Plan for roughly one to three months.

### Step 5 — Admit your first client and request the initial survey
There is no pre-licensure site visit. Within **six months** of the license effective date you must admit and serve at least one client and submit **Form 2020, Notification of Readiness for Initial Survey**, listing each client's name, admission date and service category [S5][S1]. HHSC then conducts an unannounced survey against Chapter 558.

### Step 6 — Add payers
- **Private pay:** can start as soon as the license issues.
- **HHSC PHC/CAS/FC contract:** apply to Eligibility Operations Provider Contract Management using the application and Form 5830 checklist, then complete program orientation before HHSC places you on the regional choice list [S23][S51]. Contracts follow 26 TAC Chapter 277 and Chapter 49 [S65].
- **STAR+PLUS:** enroll in Texas Medicaid and apply for credentialing with each MCO in your service area; federal rules require MCO network providers to be enrolled with the state [S56]. Set up EVV before the first Medicaid visit [S24].

### Step 7 — Renew
Renew in TULIP no later than the 45th day before expiration to avoid a late fee; an expired license means you must stop operating [S53]. The renewal fee is $2,625 for three years [S2].

sections.reimbursement:
### Private pay (the profit engine)
Families pay by the hour. CareScout's 2025 survey puts the Texas median for a non-medical caregiver at **$30 per hour** (based on 44 hours a week, about $5,720 a month), ranking Texas 43rd among states [S26]. That is a statewide figure; prices in Austin, Dallas and Houston suburbs may differ, so price from local competitors. Long-term care insurance and VA benefits often reimburse the family rather than the agency.

### STAR+PLUS (Medicaid managed care)
STAR+PLUS MCOs pay network agencies using HHSC's published attendant rates, effective September 1, 2025 [S20][S43]:

| Service | Code | Rate | Hourly |
|---|---|---|---|
| PAS, agency option (state plan, non-HCBS) | S5125 U5 | $4.40 / 15 min | $17.60 |
| PAS, agency option (HCBS) | S5125 U3 | $4.40 / 15 min | $17.60 |
| CFC PAS, agency option | S5125 U5 U7 | $4.46 / 15 min | $17.84 |
| In-home respite (HCBS) | T1005 U3 | $4.39 / 15 min | $17.56 |

Each rate splits into **$3.71 attendant cost** and an administrative component ($0.69 for PAS, $0.75 for CFC) [S20]. HHSC says the rates support an **average attendant wage of $13.00 per hour plus 14% payroll taxes and benefits** ($13.00 × 1.14 ÷ 4 = $3.71) [S20][S21]. The administrative component — **$2.76 per hour** for PAS — must pay for supervision, scheduling, EVV, billing, insurance, office and profit.

### HHSC fee-for-service: PHC, CAS and Family Care
HHSC contracts directly for Primary Home Care, Community Attendant Services and Family Care, and providers must accept HHSC's hourly rate and bill in quarter-hour increments [S23][S57]. HHSC raised these rates on September 1, 2025 under the same Rider 23 methodology, and CMS approved SPA TX-25-0005 raising the PHC attendant wage to $13.00 [S21][S40]. PHC, CAS and FC pay **$17.13 per hour** for non-priority clients and **$17.31** for priority clients ($14.82 attendant + $2.31 service support, + $0.18 priority), effective 9/1/2025 — slightly below the $17.60 STAR+PLUS PAS rate [S67]. Like STAR+PLUS, the attendant portion is built on a $13.00 average wage and 14% payroll taxes and benefits [S67], so the agency keeps $2.31–$2.49 an hour for everything else.

### What changed on September 1, 2025
- The **mandatory $10.60 base wage** for personal attendants (1 TAC §355.7051) applied only before September 1, 2025; HHSC now calls it obsolete and has proposed repealing it [S35][S36][S22]. No state rule now requires an attendant wage above the $7.25 minimum wage [S44][S45], but the rate is funded for a $13.00 average.
- The **Attendant Compensation Rate Enhancement** program and the MCO direct care enhancement programs (such as ACEP) ended August 31, 2025; their add-ons were folded into the base rate [S36][S43][S40].

### EVV and claims
EVV is required for PHC, CAS, FC, CFC and STAR+PLUS attendant services [S24]. Claims must match an accepted EVV visit on Medicaid ID, date, NPI, procedure code, modifiers and units; unmatched claims are denied or recouped [S41]. HHSC provides a cost-free EVV system (HHAeXchange), or you can use an approved proprietary system [S24][S42].

### Population
Texas had an estimated **31.7 million** residents in July 2025; **14.9%** were 65 or older (about 4.7 million people) and **8.7%** were under 65 with a disability [S49]. More than **198,000** Texans were on HHSC's six Medicaid waiver interest lists in March 2026 [S50], which signals unmet demand for long-term services, though most waiver slots go to other provider types.

### Medicaid referral pipeline
- **STAR+PLUS:** every member who receives long-term services and supports gets an MCO service coordinator, who develops the service plan and authorizes services [S63]. In practice, PAS referrals come from MCO service coordinators and from members choosing an agency, so being credentialed and responsive with each MCO matters.
- **PHC/CAS/FC:** HHSC case workers refer individuals to agencies on the regional choice list. A contracted provider must accept all referrals, finish pre-initiation activities (evaluation, service plan, practitioner's statement) within 14 days of a routine referral, and start services within 7 days after authorization [S64][S16][S17].

### Private-pay referral sources
Private clients typically come from hospital and rehab discharge planners, home health agencies, senior living communities, physicians' offices, elder-law attorneys, churches and online searches. These are standard channels, not measured volumes; no public source quantifies them for Texas.

### What we could not quantify
We found no current official count of PAS-licensed agencies, PHC/CAS/FC recipients or STAR+PLUS PAS users by region, so this report does not estimate market size or share (see "What this report does not claim").
sections.operations:
### Staffing rules
- **No staff-to-client ratios.** Chapter 558 requires written staffing policies: orientation, job-specific training, competency demonstration when education or license doesn't establish it, job descriptions, annual evaluations and signed policy acknowledgments [S10].
- **Administrator and alternate** with PAS-only qualifications [S6], 24 hours of initial training and 12 hours of annual CE [S7][S8].
- **Supervisor:** licensed nurse, or two years of college, or supervisory employment in place of college [S9]. Supervisory visit frequency is set by agency policy with client input [S9]; in PHC/CAS/FC the supervisor must make in-person visits at least annually and more often as needs require [S15]. The supervisor also does the pre-service evaluation and service delivery plan [S16].
- **Attendants:** 18+ (or a high school graduate), competency demonstrated, oriented to each client on or before the first shift, with orientation documented on a single signed form [S9][S59]. In CAS a parent can't serve a minor child, and a spouse can serve only in Family Care [S60].
- **Employability:** run the criminal history check and search the Nurse Aide Registry and Employee Misconduct Registry before hire, then search the registries at least every 12 months [S11][S48].
- **Abuse, neglect and exploitation:** investigate and self-report incidents under §558.249 [S54]; keep an emergency preparedness plan under §558.256 [S55].

### Medicaid service rules (PHC/CAS/FC)
Deliver all authorized, scheduled hours except documented interruptions, and never exceed five times the weekly authorized hours in a month [S61]. Bill only authorized tasks and hours, accept HHSC's hourly rate, and round to the quarter hour (8 minutes or more rounds up) [S57].

### Wage and hour law
Home care agencies are third-party employers, so they **cannot** use the FLSA companionship or live-in exemptions: attendants are owed minimum wage and overtime [S34]. Travel between clients during the workday is compensable [S33]. The model adds 4% paid non-billable time (operator estimate) for travel, orientation and in-service.

### Required systems
- **TULIP** for licensing [S1].
- **EVV** for every Medicaid attendant visit; the state system is free, and claims must match EVV data [S24][S41][S42].
- **Scheduling and billing software** for private pay (operator estimate in the model).

### Wages (BLS OEWS May 2025)
Home health and personal care aides: Texas median $11.65/hour (75th percentile $13.23); Houston median $11.27 (75th percentile $13.36); Dallas–Fort Worth median $12.93; Austin $13.64; San Antonio $12.48 [S30]. These May 2025 figures predate the September 2025 Medicaid rate increase, which funds a $13.00 average [S21]. Texas's minimum wage is $7.25 and cities cannot set a higher private-sector minimum [S45][S58]. Workers' compensation is elective for private employers [S19]; the new-employer unemployment tax rate is 2.70% on the first $9,000 [S25]. Office roles in the model use Houston medians: supervisor $46,350 [S32], scheduler/billing $44,210 [S29], administrator $62,330 (25th pct) to $76,780 (median) [S31].
sections.market_conditions:
### Price
Texas is a low-price home care state. The 2025 CareScout median for a non-medical caregiver is $30/hour, rank 43 of the states surveyed [S26]. Low prices squeeze private-pay margins compared with coastal states, so pricing discipline (minimum visit lengths, weekend/holiday rates) matters.

### Medicaid rates
The September 2025 increase moved the funded attendant wage from the old $10.60 base wage to a $13.00 average and raised payroll taxes and benefits to 14% for community services [S21][S36][S35]. At the same time HHSC ended the rate enhancement add-ons [S43][S40]. The resulting $4.40 per 15 minutes is the whole STAR+PLUS PAS payment [S20].

### Workforce
The OEWS May 2025 Texas median for home health and personal care aides was $11.65/hour [S30], below the $13.00 Medicaid-funded average. Private-pay agencies therefore compete for the same workers against Medicaid agencies that can now pay around $13. Austin and Dallas–Fort Worth pay more than Houston and San Antonio [S30]. Expect to pay at or above $13.

### Supply
No public, current count of PAS-licensed agencies or market shares was found; we do not estimate competition. Check the HHSC regional choice list for your area (for PHC/CAS/FC) and local search results to gauge private-pay competitors.

### Trends to watch
- The legislature funds attendant wages every two years through the GAA; Rider 23 set the current level for 2026–27 [S21].
- HHSC proposed repealing the obsolete base-wage rule in August 2026 [S22] and proposed Chapter 558 amendments in September 2026 [S14].
sections.financial_narrative:
### How the model is built
Capacity is the active client census the office is sized for; occupancy (90% default) is the share actually receiving service in a month (an operator assumption). Revenue = hourly rate × billable hours. Every configuration assumes **80 billable hours per client-month** (about 18.5 hours a week), an operator estimate inside the PHC/CAS limits of 6–50 hours a week [S18]. Attendants are paid for those 80 hours plus 4% non-billable time (travel between clients is paid time [S33]).

- **Private-pay price:** $30/hour, the CareScout Texas median [S26].
- **Medicaid price:** STAR+PLUS PAS $4.40 per 15 minutes = $17.60/hour [S20]; the PHC/CAS/FC configuration uses the HHSC non-priority rate of $17.13/hour [S67].
- **Wages:** private-pay caregivers at the Houston 75th percentile, $13.36 [S30]; Medicaid attendants at the $13.00 average the rates fund [S20][S67]; office staff at Houston OEWS medians [S29][S31][S32]. The office lease uses Houston Class B rent of $23.23 per sq ft per year [S28].
- **Payroll burden:** 15.5% (9.5% taxes [S27][S25], 3% workers' comp, 3% benefits — the last two operator estimates). That is above the 14% PTB HHSC built into the attendant rate [S20].
- **Fixed costs** include the HCSSA renewal ($2,625 ÷ 36) [S2], insurance, software, accounting, marketing and utilities (operator estimates). Franchise tax is $0 in every configuration because revenue stays under the $2.65 million no-tax-due threshold, and an HCSSA in Medicaid excludes 50% of Medicaid payments [S38][S39].

### Results at 90% occupancy
| Configuration | Monthly net | Margin | Break-even occupancy |
|---|---|---|---|
| Private pay, 40 clients | +$14,533 | 16.8% | 54% |
| Private pay, 20 clients (owner-administrator paid $62,330) | +$5,363 | 12.4% | 63% |
| Mixed 60 clients (50/50) | +$3,025 | 2.9% | 81% |
| Medicaid only, 100 clients (STAR+PLUS) | −$19,143 | −15.1% | not reachable (≈314 clients) |
| Medicaid only, 100 clients (HHSC PHC/CAS/FC) | −$22,527 | −18.3% | not reachable (≈560 clients) |
| Medicaid only, 250 clients (STAR+PLUS) | −$24,058 | −7.6% | not reachable (≈506 clients) |

### Why Medicaid-only loses money
Each Medicaid billable hour brings in $17.60. The attendant costs $13.00 × 1.04 paid-hour factor × 1.155 burden ≈ $15.62, leaving about $1.98 an hour, and per-client costs (software, insurance, recruiting, supplies, checks, mileage) take another ~$0.92. That leaves about **$86 per client per month** to cover the office. Under the HHSC PHC/CAS/FC contract the non-priority rate is $17.13 [S67], leaving about $0.59 an hour after the same costs — roughly **$48 per client per month**, so a 100-client PHC agency loses about $22,500 a month and would need about 560 clients to cover the same office. A 250-client agency breaks even only if the attendant wage falls to about **$11.90** (at $12.00 it still loses $2,436 a month; at $11.50 it earns $8,375). That is legal — no attendant wage floor has applied since September 1, 2025 [S22] — but below the $13.00 HHSC funded and harder to staff. Large Medicaid agencies make it work with very high volume, lean offices and lower benefit costs; a new agency should not count on that.

### Sensitivity (operator estimates — verify locally)
- **Caregiver wage $15.00 instead of $13.36:** private 40 nets $8,860; private 20 nets $2,527; mixed 60 loses $1,231.
- **60 billable hours per client-month instead of 80:** private 40 nets $4,488; private 20 nets $341; mixed 60 loses $5,581.
- **Private price $27 instead of $30:** private 40 nets $5,893; private 20 nets $1,043; mixed 60 loses $3,455.
- **Conservative 80% census:** private 40 nets $10,506; mixed 60 loses $253.

The private-pay result is most sensitive to hours sold per client and to the spread between price and caregiver wage.
sections.risks:
- **Thin Medicaid spread.** The STAR+PLUS PAS rate leaves $2.76 an hour for all non-attendant costs [S20]; the PHC/CAS/FC non-priority rate leaves $2.31 [S67]. Any wage pressure above $13.00, overtime, or higher workers' comp turns Medicaid hours into losses (see Section 8).
- **Wage competition.** Medicaid agencies are funded to pay a $13.00 average [S21], above the May 2025 Texas aide median of $11.65 [S30]. Private-pay agencies must pay at least that to recruit; at $15.00 the 40-client private model's profit falls by about 40%.
- **Overtime and travel time.** Agencies can't use the companionship exemption [S34]; travel between clients is paid [S33]. Poor scheduling creates overtime that the model does not include.
- **EVV denials.** Medicaid claims without a matching accepted EVV visit are denied or recouped [S41]. Budget staff time for visit maintenance.
- **Policy and rate changes.** Rates depend on biennial appropriations [S21]; the rate enhancement program was discontinued in 2025 [S36]; Chapter 558 amendments are pending [S14].
- **Licensing deadlines.** Missing the six-month Form 2020 survey request [S5] or the renewal deadline [S53] can cost you the license. An expired license means you must stop operating [S53].
- **Workers' comp is elective** [S19]. Going without coverage avoids premiums but leaves injury claims on the agency; the model includes 3% (operator estimate).
- **Payroll solvency.** HHSC rules require enough funds to meet payroll [S52]. Payers pay after the work is done, so you carry payroll during ramp-up.
- **Private-pay concentration.** A few heavy-hour clients can be a large share of revenue; a hospitalization or death cuts hours instantly.
- **Abuse, neglect and exploitation.** Investigation and self-reporting duties apply [S54]; registry checks before hire and every year are mandatory [S11][S48].
sections.recommendations:
1. **Get the PAS category, not a home health license**, unless you will provide skilled nursing or therapy. It costs the same $2,625 [S2] but has simpler administrator rules and no RN supervisor requirement [S6][S9].
2. **Launch private pay first.** The 40-client private-pay model is the only configuration that is solidly profitable at default assumptions (+$14,533 a month). Start owner-operated (the 20-client model nets about $5,400 a month on top of a $62,330 administrator salary) and add a supervisor and scheduler as census passes 20.
3. **Protect the spread.** Price at or above the $30 Texas median [S26] after checking local competitors, set minimum visit lengths (for example 4 hours) to keep billable hours near 80 per client-month, and charge more for weekends, holidays and short-notice care. Pay caregivers competitively (at least $13–$15) to keep turnover down.
4. **Add Medicaid as fill-in volume, not the core.** Once the office is paid for by private pay, STAR+PLUS PAS hours add a small contribution per hour. Credential with the MCOs in your area and set up EVV first [S56][S24]. The HHSC PHC/CAS/FC contract pays $17.13 (non-priority) or $17.31 (priority) an hour [S67] — less than STAR+PLUS — so treat it as a referral source to add after STAR+PLUS, not a reason to open [S23].
5. **Meet the Day-1 compliance items.** Presurvey Training before applying [S3], administrator training [S7], service plans and supervisor visits [S9][S15], orientation before every first shift [S59], and registry checks before hire [S11].
6. **Request the initial survey early.** Admit your first private client, then file Form 2020 well inside the six-month window [S5].
7. **Keep three to six months of fixed costs in reserve.** Rules require you to make payroll [S52], and each configuration runs a deficit during ramp-up.

corrections_vs_previous: Old document said the Texas Department of State Health Services (DSHS) licenses HCSSAs. Licensing is done by HHSC Long-term Care Regulation through the TULIP portal (HHSC HCSSA Initial Licensure; 26 TAC Ch. 558).

Old document told applicants to request a 'Licensed Home Care Services' category. No such category exists; the six categories in 26 TAC §558.13(b) include 'personal assistance services', which is the correct category for non-medical personal care.

Old document said to 'contract with HHSC for waiver-based programs (STAR+PLUS, MDCP)'. STAR+PLUS is managed care: agencies credential with each MCO, and MCO service coordinators authorize PAS. The HHSC contract is for Primary Home Care, Community Attendant Services and Family Care (26 TAC Ch. 277; HHSC 'What is PHC?').
Old document listed workers' compensation insurance as a requirement. Coverage is elective for Texas private employers (Labor Code §406.002).

Old timeline described an HCSSA application that 'includes … survey' before licensure. The survey happens after licensure: admit at least one client and file Form 2020 within six months (26 TAC §558.521); HHSC processing is 45 days to completeness plus 45 days to issue (§558.31).

Old P&L used an unsourced '$35/hour tier rate' for Medicaid home care. STAR+PLUS PAS pays $4.40 per 15 minutes ($17.60/hour), CFC PAS $4.46, effective 9/1/2025 (HHSC PFD rate sheet). Texas has no 'tier' PAS rates.

Old P&L assumed 6 hours a day × 30 days per participant and showed $85,400 a month for 10 clients; at its own $35 rate that arithmetic gives $63,000, and 180 hours a month per client is not a typical authorization. The new model uses 80 billable hours per client-month, labeled an operator estimate, within the 6–50 hour weekly PHC/CAS limits (40 TAC §48.2918).

Old P&L paid caregivers $16.50/hour with no source, set administrator salary at $0 and included no payroll taxes. The new model uses $13.00 (the Medicaid-funded average) or the Houston 75th-percentile OEWS wage of $13.36 for private pay, Houston OEWS office salaries, and 15.5% payroll burden.

Old document said all staff need CPR/first aid. 26 TAC §558.404 requires competency (and an RN-led program for g-tube feedings and medication administration); no CPR mandate was found in Chapter 558 — it is listed as not verified.

Old document left out Presurvey Training before applying (§558.13(a)), the 24-hour administrator training (§558.259), PAS-only administrator qualifications (§558.244(a)(3)), supervisor qualifications (§558.404(g)), EVV and EVV claims matching, the September 2025 end of the attendant base-wage rule and rate enhancement program, and the license-exempt status of companion-only services (HSC §142.003(a)(15)).
